articles.title: Company video: what to prepare before filming
articles.coverAlt: Company video: what to prepare before filming
articles.description: Before you film a video for your company, prepare the goal, audience, script and location. Practical tips that save time and money.
articles.body:
A company video is one of the strongest ways to build customer trust, but a good video starts with preparation, not filming day. These are the points to settle before the camera starts.

## 1. Decide the goal of the video

Do you want to introduce the company, advertise a product or explain a service? Each goal needs a different style and length. A short ad is not the same as a longer introduction video.

## 2. Know your audience

Are you talking to individual customers or to companies? The tone, music and length all change with the audience. Think about where the video will be watched: Facebook, Instagram, YouTube or your website.

## 3. Write a simple idea and script

It doesn't have to be complicated. One page with the scenes in order and the main sentence you want the viewer to leave with is enough. It saves time in filming and editing.

## 4. Prepare the place and the people

Choose a tidy place with good lighting, and make sure the people who appear in the video know the filming time and dress suitably. Small details like these change the result.

## 5. Think about editing and delivery

Ask from the start what size and format you will receive, and whether you need versions for mobile and social media. Also decide who will write the subtitles if the video needs them.

articles.title: How to run a successful live stream for your conference or event
articles.coverAlt: How to run a successful live stream for your conference or event
articles.description: Practical steps for a successful live stream at a conference, sports tournament or event in Egypt: internet, cameras, sound and what to prepare before the day.
articles.body:
Live streaming is now normal at conferences, sports tournaments and corporate events, because it lets people who can't attend watch the moment as it happens. But a good stream takes more than a camera and a phone. It needs preparation before the day.

## 1. The internet matters more than the camera

The most common problem that ruins a stream is weak internet. Ask the venue about the upload speed, not the download speed. If the hall is weak, ask for a dedicated line for the stream or prepare a backup line. A stream needs a stable connection more than a fast one.

## 2. Sound is half the picture

People forgive a picture that isn't perfect, but not choppy or echoing sound. Use a separate microphone for the speaker or the host, and take a direct feed from the sound system if the hall has a mixer.

## 3. More than one camera makes a difference

One camera gives you a working stream. Two or three let you switch between angles like TV, which matters most at conferences and tournaments. Agree early on who controls the switching.

## 4. Choose the right platform

YouTube suits conferences and events people will watch later. Facebook and Instagram suit you if your audience is there. A stream can go out to more than one platform at the same time.

## 5. Test before the day

Do a rehearsal at the same place with the same internet and equipment. A rehearsal shows lighting, sound and connection problems while you still have time to fix them.

articles.title: Tips for better conference and event photos
articles.coverAlt: Tips for better conference and event photos
articles.description: Simple tips for better conference and event photos: a shot list, lighting, agreeing with your photographer before the day, and delivery.
articles.body:
Event photos stay with you and get used on social media, in press and in reports, so they are worth preparing for. These simple tips make a big difference to the photos you get.

## 1. Agree with the photographer before the event

Tell the photographer how the photos will be used: social media, a report or ads. Decide which shots must be taken: speakers, audience, sponsors and key moments.

## 2. Make a list of important shots and people

Write down the people who must be photographed: guests, speakers, sponsors and the team. In the rush of an event many people get forgotten, and a list makes sure nobody is missed.

## 3. Lighting matters

Visit the venue before the day and agree on the lighting with the photographer so the photos don't come out dark, especially on stage and in halls.

## 4. Set aside time for posed shots

During the event, set aside a few minutes for group shots and speaker portraits, and leave the rest of the time for candid shots.

## 5. Agree on delivery

Ask how you will receive the photos: how many, in what quality and when. If you need quick photos to publish the same day, say so from the start.
